common_name: Excellent Croton (Large-Leaf Multi-Color Cluster IV Croton)

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Excellent belongs to the large-leaved 'Cluster IV' group of croton cultivars and needs strong light to hold its color.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Excellent produces some of the largest leaves in the croton trade, broad oval blades often exceeding 12 inches long that combine green, yellow, red, and purple in a bold multicolor pattern typical of the large-leaved 'Cluster IV' croton group that also includes Petra. Give it the brightest available light to intensify coloring, since leaves grown in shade revert toward plain green with age. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance and drops leaves readily below 50°F.

common_name: Sunny Star Croton (Narrow Yellow-Mottled Strap-Leaf Croton)

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Sunny Star's yellow variegation is best in a bright, sunny to semi-sunny spot rather than deep shade.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Sunny Star carries narrow, glossy, lance-shaped leaves that emerge light green and mature to a deeper green heavily overlaid with bright yellow spots, mottling, or blotches, a strap-leaf pattern closer to Zanzibar or Banana in form but far more heavily yellow than either. Morning or late-day sun, or a bright winter exposure, produces the strongest yellow coloring, while low light causes the leaves to green over. Keep the root ball evenly and lightly moist, and keep the plant above 59°F, since it is even more cold-sensitive than most crotons.

common_name: Norma Croton (Subdued Green Croton with Colored Veining)

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Norma is a subdued, primarily green-leaved croton grown for its colored veining rather than bold leaf color.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Norma was bred in Italy by the Azienda Gloreal Diem nursery from a cross of 'Bravo' and 'Ernestine Delarue' and later introduced to the United States trade by Kraft Nursery of Boca Raton; its oval leaves emerge yellow, pass through green, and finally settle into a deep wine-red, staying mostly green with yellow or red venation along the way rather than displaying the bold multicolor blotching of showier crotons. It is markedly more shade-tolerant than most named crotons, growing acceptably from full sun into fairly deep shade, though the wine-red final color is strongest with more light. Water regularly to keep the soil evenly moist, since Norma tolerates neither drought nor waterlogging, and protect from frost.
sources: Palmpedia Palm and Cycad Grower's Guide

common_name: Bush on Fire Croton (Compact Fire-Toned Croton)

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; Bush on Fire is a compact, fire-toned selection well suited to smaller pots and terrariums.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light rather than harsh direct sun. Bush on Fire is a compact croton whose narrow leaves shift from green through yellow into intense red and orange as they mature, giving a densely packed, fiery two-tone look on a smaller-statured plant than most landscape crotons. Its compact habit and tolerance of high humidity make it a popular choice for terrariums, bright bathrooms, and other close-in container plantings. Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, provide high humidity for the cleanest color, and protect from any frost.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Mona Lisa Croton (Creamy Yellow-Center Dark-Margin Croton)

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Mona Lisa is a slow-growing selection best suited to smaller pots and tighter spaces.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Mona Lisa, developed by hobbyist breeder Rudy Bachmann, bears broad leaves dominated by a rich, creamy yellow center bordered by a narrow dark green margin, a simpler two-tone pattern that reads as more refined and less busy than heavily multicolor cultivars like Petra. Its slow growth rate keeps plants compact for years, making it a good choice where a smaller croton is wanted without frequent pruning. Water when the top inch of soil dries, provide bright light to keep the yellow center vivid, and protect from any frost.
sources: Palmpedia Palm and Cycad Grower's Guide

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Dreadlocks is a slow-growing, strongly weeping cultivar best given room to cascade.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Dreadlocks, an introduction from Emerald Goddess Gardens, produces long, narrow, ruffled leaves that twist and cascade like dreadlocks, opening green before shifting through bright yellow and bronze-burgundy with paint-splattered speckles of yellow, peach, red, and orange as they age. Growth is notably slower than in most crotons, so plants stay a manageable 3 to 4 feet even after years in the ground or a large pot, and the pendulous habit is best shown off in a hanging basket or raised bed where the leaves can drape freely. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.

common_name: Sloppy Painter Croton (Random Splashed Multi-Color Croton)

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sloppy Painter is hardy in USDA zones 9b through 11 and needs bright light to hold its splashed coloring.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Sloppy Painter carries narrow green leaves overlaid with irregular streaks and speckles of yellow, red, orange, and occasionally pink, scattered across each leaf in a random, paint-splattered pattern rather than the more orderly veining or banding seen in cultivars like Mrs. Iceton. Give it at least six to eight hours of bright light daily to keep the color pattern vivid, and prune every six to eight weeks if a denser, more compact shrub is wanted. Maintain consistent moisture and high humidity, and protect from any frost, since this selection has the same cold sensitivity as other named crotons.
sources: Port St. Lucie Botanical Gardens cultivar reference

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Aucubaefolia is one of the oldest named croton cultivars still in general cultivation.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Aucubaefolia bears thick, glossy, oval to elongated green leaves scattered with irregular gold speckles, a sparser and more randomly scattered spotting pattern than the fine, dense stippling of Gold Dust, and its name and look both reference the similarly gold-speckled foliage of Aucuba japonica. This is a long-cultivated, heirloom-type croton selection that has remained in the nursery trade for well over a century thanks to its reliable, easy-to-grow habit. Bright light produces the most speckling; water when the top inch of soil dries, and protect from any frost.

planting.note: Plant container specimens after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Curly Boy is grown chiefly for its twisted, corkscrewed leaf form.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Curly Boy produces thick, leathery, narrowly lance-shaped leaves that twist and curl along their length, opening bright green and maturing to shades of maroon, red, pink, and orange, giving the plant a dense, textural look distinct from the flat-leaved forms of Petra or Mammy. Its dense, multi-branched, upright habit reaching 6 to 8 feet makes it useful as an informal hedge, screen, or accent shrub in frost-free landscapes, in addition to container and houseplant use. Water when the top inch of soil dries, provide ample bright light for the strongest color, and protect from any frost.
